After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

T here are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration , Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia , which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along anyone human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang, and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Payton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

stories.title: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
stories.summary: Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.

stories.body:
Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.

On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people said.

Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board said it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a company executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

Allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

Their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A company “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.

“He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

“He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

“The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions.”

Others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

Published 2 hours ago

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's goodlooking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 9 hours ago

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump Published 20 hours ago

US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation Published 6 hours ago

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

Nvidia's shares fall 5% at the open

Nvidia’s shares are dropping at the start of trading in New York, as the rally following the return of Jensen Huang yesterday subsides.

Nvidia has fallen by 5.5% in the first couple of minutes of trading, to $155.87. That erodes a small portion of yesterday’s 32% surge.

The chipmaker’s stock is under pressure amid criticism of Huang’s return from both Republicans and Democrats.

Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans, warns that reinstating Huang could backfire:

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Closing summary

Time to wrap up…

The sell-off in US tech stocks has resumed, as Monday’s relief rally following the reappointment of Jensen Huang to run Nvidia quickly faded.

Shares in Nvidia are down 7.7% at $152.35, wiping out around a third of Monday’s jump.

Anthropic , the frontier AI firm which floated last week, are down 9.75% at $79.08, meaning anyone who took part in its IPO (priced at $83 a share) is facing a loss.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, says:

double quotation mark “The loss of the $83 IPO price is a major development, coming so swiftly after the listing. By comparison it was a month before SpaceX suffered the same fate. Launching a major IPO in the midst of one of the biggest tech selloffs of recent times was never going to be great timing, but there was a growing sense of ‘now or never’. Huang’s return seems to have amplified the instinct to sell, given his love for open source models rather than the paid version, and absent a broader market recovery it seems Anthropic is fated to struggle for now.”

This is pulling the wider US market into the red, with the Nasdaq Composite now down 2%.

That has punctured an early feeling of relief in the markets, where Asia-Pacific bourses generally rallied today .

Stocks are sliding amid a backlash to the decision to reappoint Huang, under pressure from the White House.

Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with president Trump.”

And Bernie Sanders has warned AI firms not to expect a bailout if their investments go wrong.

Huang will make several several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China

Our US Politics Live blog is keeping tabs on the latest developments:

The rapid expansion of AI data centre construction could exacerbate the US housing shortage by drawing workers away from homebuilding.

Oxford Economics has estimated that up to 45,000 additional workers would be employed in residential construction across the 10 states with the highest data centre spending had employment trends followed those elsewhere in the country.

Matthew Martin , senior US economist at Oxford Economics , explains:

double quotation mark “Data centre projects appear to be bidding up wages. “As data centre demand shows little sign of slowing, the wider premium may make it harder for homebuilders to compete for workers.”

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo , Professor Dame Wendy Hall , Stuart J. Russell and Alexandra Birch-Mayne as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

Book tickets here or at guardian.live

The S&P 500, the flagship US share index, is down 0.4% in early trading at 7,206 points.

But.. the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 0.4%. reaching 49,795 points. Twenty three of the 30 stocks on the DJIA are up, while Nvidia (-5.5%) is the top faller.

The tech-focused Nasdaq index has opened lower too – it’s down 1.8% at 23,661 points.

Analog Devices (-15%) are the top faller, followed by chipmaker AMD (-10.1%) and SanDisk Corporation (-9.2%).

Anthropic's shares tumble below IPO price

Oof! Anthropic’s share price has tumbled below the level at which the frontier AI company sold shares to investors last week, in its record-breaking float.

Anthropic’s stock has dropped by 8.3% at the start of trading, to $80.34, below the $83 IPO price.

This may sour demand for AI-linked stocks, warns Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

She explains:

double quotation mark A drop below $83 so quickly after its IPO could also weigh on the future earnings reports of its largest backers. For example, if Anthropic’s share price falls sharply, then Google and Alphabet, which hold just under 30% of the stock, could take a hit to their bottom lines. So far, Alphabet and Amazon are posting relatively small losses on Tuesday, but these could worsen if Anthropic’s share price continues to decline.

Nvidia’s shares are dropping at the start of trading in New York, as the rally following the return of Jensen Huang yesterday subsides.

Nvidia has fallen by 5.5% in the first couple of minutes of trading, to $155.87. That erodes a small portion of yesterday’s 32% surge.

The chipmaker’s stock is under pressure amid criticism of Huang’s return from both Republicans and Democrats.

Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans, warns that reinstating Huang could backfire:

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Bernie Sanders: Taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech oligarchs.

Democratic senator Bernie Sanders has warned US tech companies not to expect a bailout if their AI investments turn sour.

Posting on X , Sanders says:

double quotation mark One thing must be made certain: If the AI bubble bursts, taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech Oligarchs. Not tomorrow. Not next year. Not ever. If AI companies fail, Big Tech Oligarchs must bail them out, not taxpayers. Our message to these multi-billionaires is simple: If you take out a loan, pay it back. Don’t come begging to taxpayers to bail you out.

WSJ: US prepares to raise tariffs on China and other countries

Fears of a new US-China trade war are rippling through the markets today too.

The Wall Street Journal are reporting that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, according to people familiar with the plans.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could release the results of a tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations later this week, the WSJ adds…..

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene has warned that UK interest rates need to keep rising, unless there is a “miraculous” breakthough in the Middle East conflict.

Speaking in London today, Greene – one of the more hawkish members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee – warned that the BOE is “a little bit behind the curve now.”

She explained:

double quotation mark “I think it’s appropriate to tighten policy further unless there’s a miraculous turnaround in data or in the war.”

The City money markets indicate there’s an 84% chance that the Bank rises interest rates at its next meeting, in mid-December.

Most stock markets in the Gulf region posted gains today, taking their cue from Wall Street yesterday, and then Asia-Pacific markets overnight.

Saudi Arabia’s ⁠benchmark index gained 0.4%, while Dubai’s main share index rose by 0.8%, ​ Abu Dhabi’s market finished 1% higher, and Qatar posted a 0.75% rise.

Meta launches AI assistant Muse - are you planning to use it?

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on their apps – and the high street.

Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.

Meta says:

double quotation mark “From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you.”

So… we’d like to know if you have plans to try Muse, or if you’re already a user. Let us know here :

Meanwhile in the bond markets, the UK has paid a record high price to sell inflation-linked bonds.

Britain’s Debt Management Office sold £3.75bn of an index-linked gilt which matures in 2049, at a real yield (the return after inflation) of 2.5235%. That, Reuters has calculated, is the highest for a syndicated sale since records began in 2005.

But, Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen points out that there are ‘clear differences’ with the other big risk-off moves of the last decade:

First, there wasn’t a sudden and fundamental reassessment of the growth outlook, like when the pandemic began in 2020, or during the Liberation Day selloff of 2025.

stories.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
stories.summary: Some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

The government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public to "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

Writing in the Guardian, , external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women."

He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse".

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada , external the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

Recent high-profile cases including Russell Brand's rape conviction and allegations made against David Walliams have prompted conversations about both the age of consent and NDAs.

Mia Latter, a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, has called for the age of consent to be changed.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

In the same week that Brand was convicted, ITV News and the Guardian reported that David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

In late 2023, Walliams' publisher HarperCollins started an internal inquiry about the author's alleged inappropriate behaviour with young female staff.

A female staff member left the company with a pay-out and an NDA.

A spokesperson for the publisher has said: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams.

"We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."

stories.title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
stories.summary: "Without this funding, activities would be delayed."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“Without this funding, activities would be delayed.”

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government ( PDF ).

The list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”

The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

Another continuing resolution?

Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

Given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the new year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

Flexibility for Isaacman

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission plan that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test issues.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

“Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

stories.body:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures , regulatory proceedings , and the courts . The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976 , which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709 .

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives , meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors , while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users .

What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves , since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies " de-identify " age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives —meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize ) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends , support groups , community organizing , local news , creative audiences , and ways to speak out on current issues . U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information , and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice . Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth , however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Help Us Help You

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate . If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org .

Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

Anthony Albanese and Matthew Wale sign new treaty as Solomon Islands PM states his country no longer ‘a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region’

The Solomon Islands prime minister says the days of his country being an uncertain partner in the Pacific are over as he signed a sweeping agreement to make Australia the primary security partner and limit ties with China.

Matthew Wale signed the new treaty with Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese , in Canberra on Wednesday after Solomon Islands earlier this week announced it was terminating a landmark security pact with Beijing.

The treaty is a blow to China’s efforts to build influence with Pacific Island nations and a major win for the Albanese government’s campaign to rebuild ties across the region.

“Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done. Gone. We don’t want to be there again,” Wale told reporters.

The deal means Solomon Islands will not allow foreign military bases or major security infrastructure to be developed on its territory. Sensitive systems will remain “free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access”.

In exchange, Honiara has secured new funding for policing services and improved visa arrangements, allowing Solomon Islands citizens to stay in Australia for longer periods and take advantage of employment opportunities in early childhood education and aged care.

Australia and Solomon Islands have agreed to advance joint economic, development and security priorities, with Australia pledging to invest in community development, education and infrastructure.

Australia will also increase funding for the Solomon Kings Football Club, including player development.

“This treaty will strengthen our security partnership,” Albanese said.

“Australia is proud to be Solomon Islands’ main security partner, and that’s a responsibility that we take seriously. We’ll continue working with Solomon Islands to keep its community safe, to strengthen its police force and improve border security.

“We’ll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions.”

Wale said secrecy provisions prevented him from speaking publicly when asked about ending the pact with Beijing. The five-year deal was due to expire in April and will not be renewed.

“We have ongoing discussions with China, but of course today is about our relationship with Australia and the treaty that we’ve signed,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

Albanese welcomed more than 15 Solomon Island cabinet ministers as part of the official delegation visiting Canberra. Their presence and Wale’s confidence at surviving any fresh no confidence motions in parliament signalled the stronger relationship could last.

Albanese and senior Australian ministers including Penny Wong, Pat Conroy and Richard Marles stepped up engagement in the Pacific after Labor’s election win in 2022. Labor has signed new alliances and agreements with countries including Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Fiji.

Asked about the termination of the Solomon Islands deal, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday that no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation existed in Beijing’s cooperation with the Pacific.

“China always follows the principle of mutual respect and equality in developing relations with the Solomon Islands.

“Our cooperation does not target any third party and is not subject to third-party influence.”

China’s embassy in Canberra was contacted for comment.

Published 24 November 2026

Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

BBC Newsnight special on nuclear test veterans

Victoria Derbyshire speaks to veterans as an independent panel is announced into health impacts

Watch now on iPlayer

Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.

Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.

Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.

The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the LABRATS group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.

Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.

Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers.

He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years.

"Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."

This video can not be played

Watch: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about search for justice

Barbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.

She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."

Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.

He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."

Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.

On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of.

"Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told campaigners in Downing Street that he would launch an independent investigation

The MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.

However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026 , though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.

'Serious allegations against the state'

The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.

He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."

Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."

He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit.

stories.title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
stories.summary: Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app. Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “ Intelligent Screen Context ,” while Apple refers to it as either “ Onscreen Awareness ” or “ Visual Intelligence .” Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option. While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

stories.body:
Tariffs are a signature policy of Trump's office

Published 2 hours ago

The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan among the 16 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit the US accused China of not fully living up the terms of what it agreed in South Korea in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

stories.body:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change , which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN ), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation ) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration ( issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.

stories.body:
South Africa’s local government elections in November 2026 drew attention to the role of mayors in municipal government, particularly in Johannesburg. However, Johannesburg’s mayoralty has a long history, with more than 100 mayors having occupied the chair. Christopher McMichael and Philip Harrison have just published a book, Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City . Harrison answers questions about it.

You wrote the book amid a deepening governance crisis. How does the book speak to this?

The book doesn’t try to solve – or even dissect – the current crisis . Instead, it steps back to view Johannesburg and its governance through the long lens of history.

Cities swing between growth, crisis and stagnation; a single snapshot never tells the whole story. We think history offers hope: circumstances shift.

Taking the long view matters for another reason too. Cities are the product of a complex layering of multiple processes with different time horizons. Johannesburg’s crumbling infrastructure is a prime example. While the past decade’s unstable coalitions have accelerated the decay, essential assets like water, power and road infrastructure are built to last 30 years or more – meaning their current state reflects decades of neglect.

Understanding history transforms how we experience the present.

What were the good years, and what were the bad?

One group’s golden age may be another’s darkest hour. This was, for example, the case in the 1950s and 1960s when the white middle class was realising the benefits of an American-type suburban lifestyle while the Black residents of townships were experiencing heightened state repression.

Nevertheless, some periods are associated with narratives of progress, and others with crisis or stagnation. The optimism in the late 1930s is a case in point.

The Great Depression was followed by a mining boom, with the central business district going high-rise, and new infrastructure laid out across the city. Johannesburg celebrated its golden jubilee in 1936 with the Empire Exhibition , cementing its status as a new and prosperous City of Empire.

Another period of optimism, for white Johannesburg at least, was the early 1970s. The United Party-controlled city council declared an era of civic progress with the construction of a vast network of motorways, the opening of the Carlton Centre as Africa’s tallest building, and a grand new civic centre.

The celebratory mood, of course, ended when the youth in Soweto rose in revolt in June 1976 .

Other moments of hope came in the early 1990s, as the political impasse of the previous decade ended, although the transition was turbulent. The 2000s saw at least a decade of rapid economic growth, though governance controversies persisted.

But there were certainly bad times: the South African War (1899-1902); a bitter struggle between white capital and white labour which culminated in the Rand Rebellion ; two world wars, the influenza pandemic, the Great Depression, and the shock of the Afrikaner nationalist victory of 1948.

The 1980s may have been the city’s low point. A conservative coalition of the National Party and the Independent Ratepayers Association resisted desegregation. It planned to celebrate Johannesburg’s centenary in 1986, but the then president, P.W. Botha, declared a nationwide state of emergency .

The transition in the 1990s was a roller coaster, ending with a financial crisis that nearly bankrupted the city. Over the past ten years or so, the city has seen unstable coalition governments, deteriorated service delivery, and increasing corruption, along with the COVID-19 pandemic and a stagnant economy.

It is a complex story of hope and despair, driven by an entanglement of local and national factors, but it does suggest a city of some resilience.

Why does the mayor matter in all of this?

In the colonial and apartheid years, mayors were ceremonial, elected for single-year terms, with governing left mainly to council committees. Mayors generally acted as a stabilising force, mediating in back rooms between competing interests.

From 2000, with the introduction of the executive mayoralty , mayors mattered far more directly. They led the executive branch and could drive a vision for the city.

From 2019, mayors had to cede power to coalition partners to remain in office. The city administration became a patchwork of fiefdoms.

Mayors, whether ceremonial or executive, make the complexity of city governance visible to the public. However, the mayor is only one of many actors in city administration. Bureaucrats, councillors, union heads and many others play crucial roles.

While we have used the mayor as a lens into city administration, we recognise its limitations. The book tries to contextualise the work of mayors within a much wider landscape of change.

Were there good mayors, and what measures define success?

Good and “bad” are subjective concepts. But we do have a definition of “good” for the colonial and apartheid eras, and for the post-apartheid period.

Before 1994, a “good mayor” was one who pushed the bounds of convention towards a fairer society. White Joburg society was quite conservative overall, and a radically progressive politician was unlikely to become mayor. Nevertheless, there were individuals who tried in their limited ways: Edwin Orlando Leake, who was concerned with housing opportunities for African people; Maurice Freeman, who defended Indian people from discriminatory legislation; Max Goodman, who defied police orders in engaging with protestors; Alec Jaffe, who tried to protect vulnerable tenants from unscrupulous landlords; Monty Sklaar, who promoted multi-racialism in council events.

The most consequential “good mayor” may have been Johannesburg’s first woman mayor, Jessie McPherson, elected in 1945 and representing the Labour Party. She clashed with segregationists and was subjected to a travel ban by the national government for 15 years.

The good mayors were outnumbered by the bad ones, who entrenched civic exclusion and local prejudice.

This leaves us to ask what a good mayor may be in the post-apartheid period; perhaps one who put the promise of making citizens’ lives better into effect.

The first black mayor, Isaac Mogase, served during the transitional period of the 1990s, and with his integrity and steady demeanour, provided confidence in local government. Amos Masondo, the first executive mayor of metropolitan Johannesburg, benefited from ten years of office, but his discipline, sense of duty and consistent administrative action, even if humdrum at times, was revealed in visible implementation. The transformation of Soweto during his mayoralty was a case in point. Parks Tau introduced progressive city policies, but implementation was limited as he lost the election to Herman Mashaba after five years.

Mashaba, in turn, promised to turn the city into a construction site within 12 to 18 months , but he underestimated the political and technical requirements for achieving this. After Mashaba, a quick succession of eight mayoralties followed (excluding one declared illegal by the high courts).

Based on your sweep of the city’s history, what takeaways do you offer?

We don’t offer explicit takeaways. But we can draw a few suggestions from our work.

One concerns the mayoral system itself. The indirectly elected executive mayor was quite successful in the first 15 or so years of post-apartheid rule. But not anymore.

Because of the instability created by coalition governance, the mayoralty needs a rethink. There are at least two options here.

The first would be to adopt a system of directly elected executive mayors, separating the mayor from the chaos of coalition politics.

Alternatively, some form of non-executive mayoralty could be considered. The mayor would be enjoined to remain above party politics and be a unifying figure.

Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City was published by Jacana Press .
