stories.body:
If approved, the money will go to Hadrian Automation to build a dozen factories for defense production. The company recently received a major investment from Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm.

In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.?

We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team.

Robert Faturechi

Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.

The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.

Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.

Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.

It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which Hadrian specializes in.

In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits and risks.)

At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder, Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-one problem that the Navy’s identified is we can’t find enough skilled workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” he told reporters . The factory will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.

The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”

Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion — more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook.

When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow. A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval vessels.” Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just $6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation. Hadrian executives told Forbes in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but outside estimates put it at a few hundred. This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa, Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January. The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years. A submarine model is displayed beneath a large U.S. flag during a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Hadrian submarine component facility in Barton, Alabama, in March. Dan Busey/The TimesDaily via AP A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and funded by Congress, some former defense officials said. The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense contractors and other private-sector businesses. But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government. When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial applications.” The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on their capital investment. David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its size. A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to allow it to continue issuing new loans. “OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said. “Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that exceed its mandate.” Read More The White House Intervened to Get a $620 Million Deal for a Company Tied to Donald Trump Jr. In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has shown a personal interest in defense tech and has criticized cronyism in defense spending. The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company. Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time, Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president, ProPublica previously reported . After defense officials got the White House request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a matter of weeks. The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played no role in the deal.

stories.title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
stories.summary: The post At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A group of climate protesters with pieces of tape reading “act” placed over their mouths hold up handwritten signs reading “shame,” “shame!” and “step up” during an indoor demonstration.
stories.body:
Carbon Captured

Amid a bitter standoff over how to stop global warming and pay for its damages, oil-producing nations blocked mention of phasing out fossil fuels, instead pressing to expand carbon capture technology.

A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.

Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.

Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.

“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday.

As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.

Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.

By Thursday, as formal climate talks continued, drafters had entirely stripped out mention of a transition away from fossil fuels while leaving the aggressive carbon capture benchmarks intact. When a final draft was proposed Sunday — two days after negotiations were scheduled to conclude — the CCS targets had been made less specific but remained, described as a nonbinding “gigatonne scale” goal.

The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.

A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.

For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.

Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.

For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.

In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.”

Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.”

But Saudi Arabia, speaking on behalf of the 22 countries in the League of Arab States, insisted CCS was an essential part of a “package of solutions” to address climate change.

“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important,” the Saudi delegate said, “it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions, which is what this COP was meant to represent, will be taken off the table.”

stories.title: Would Spain Again Say No to the Next Major Attack on Iran?
stories.summary: The right-wing and far-right parties want to make nice with Trump. The post Would Spain Again Say No to the Next Major Attack on Iran? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Secretary-General of the PSOE Pedro Sanchez (left), and the leader of the PP Alberto Nuñez Feijoo (right), during a televised head-to-head debate (Shutterstock)

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez put a direct question to the leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and his principal rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in Spain’s November 19 election debate. Did Feijóo regret his and PP’s No. 2 candidate Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo’s backing for Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran?

Sánchez called the Iran war ‘disastrous,” invoking an equally disastrous precedent in Iraq more than 20 years ago. The question deliberately pointed to a PP government, led by the prime minister José María Aznar, that was one of the key champions of that misbegotten adventure.

Instead of responding directly, Feijóo took a convoluted detour by first claiming that Sanchez was the “only sitting MP who supported a war” by endorsing the Spanish parliament military intervention in Libya in 2011. But the intervention in Libya was backed by 336 members of the Spanish Congress, including those of Feijóo’s PP, several of whom are still in parliament.

Then Feijóo brought up unrelated matters, like the migration crisis in Ceuta earlier this year, before finally answering on the Iran war: “Of course I’m against it.” He then immediately added that Iran was “a dictatorship” and that Hamas and Hezbollah were “delighted” with Sánchez.

Sanchez missed an opportunity to press his rival on whether he would let the United States use the Spanish bases at Rota and Morón for another round of strikes on Iran should such a request come from Washington.

He had solid grounds for insisting on obtaining clear answers.

When the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026, Álvarez de Toledo, Feijóo’s number two, expressed strong support for the operation and urged Spain and Europe to back it unequivocally. Former PP Prime Minister Aznar argued in March that a war to change Iran’s regime was justified. His neoconservative foundation, FAES (Fundación para el Análisis y los Estudios Sociales), still influential in parts of the PP, portrayed Sánchez’s opposition to the war as “ hypocritical and detrimental” to Spain.

Feijóo’s himself argued that Spain should preserve its relationship with Washington and put human rights ahead of international law in his criticism of Sánchez’s response to the war. Curiously, he and his party are considerably less insistent on human rights when it comes to close partners of the West, such as Israel or United Arab Emirates.

What Madrid would do in the case of another request for action by Washington depends not only on PP’s position but also on how much Feijóo would need the far-right party Vox after the November 29 election. The latest polls show that PP and Vox combined enjoy the support of almost half of the voters, while only around 40 percent favor the left bloc. The situation is in flux but the right and the far right could plausibly win an outright parliamentary majority.

Vox leader Santiago Abascal was straightforward in his support for Trump and Netanyahu. In April, he defended the U.S.–Israeli offensive as an exercise in pursuing national interests, while claiming, without citing any evidence, that the Iranian regime has killed 50,000 people and threatens the world with nuclear weapons.

The overlap between parts of PP and Vox has a history. Rafael Bardají, the Aznar adviser who pressed Spain to back the Iraq War, later joined Vox’s leadership team. In March 2026, he offered unconditional support for the U.S.- Israel war and attacked European leaders for failing to join it.

Bardají has spent years advocating for Israel and pressing for a harder line on Iran. He has served as the executive director of the Friends of Israel Initiative , a Madrid-based lobbying group that was launched in 2010 and led by Aznar, and that counts Iran ultra-hawks, such as John Bolton , among its co-founders. Bardaji also cultivated ties with neoconservative groups, like the UK-based Henry Jackson Society and the Washington DC-based Foundation for the Defense of Democracies.

A decision to allow the United States to use the Spanish bases in Rota and Morón or Spanish airspace to attack Iran would not be popular. In a March poll, 68 percent of Spaniards opposed the strikes and 53 percent backed the decision to deny the United States use of the bases for them.

A Feijóo government could reverse that position while continuing to say that it opposes war. A future U.S. request might concern refueling, transit, or logistical support. Madrid could authorize it while framing it as routine cooperation with an ally. This is the position taken by the center-right government in neighboring Portugal, which authorized the U.S. use of its airbase in the Azores islands while avoiding an open endorsement of the war.

The German Marshall Fund, a think-tank focusing on transatlantic relations, predicts that a PP-led government will take a more permissive stance on the use of the bases as part of an effort to repair relations with Washington. Feijóo’s own Atlanticist instincts—along with fear of Trump’s threats , the lingering influence of Aznar’s neoconservatism, and pressure from the ambitious hawks in his own party, such as Álvarez de Toledo and Madrid’s regional president Isabel Ayuso —would also likely push him in that direction. Vox, though more likely to focus its coalition bargaining on concerns like immigration and domestic policy, would reinforce these tendencies.

The choice would matter beyond Spain. Madrid has been one of the few European capitals willing to translate objections to U.S. and Israeli policy into concrete decisions: refusal to cooperate in any shape or form on the U.S. attack on Iran, an arms embargo on Israel, and the diplomatic recognition of Palestine. Reversing even one of those decisions would weaken Spain’s international standing and turn Madrid from a point of resistance to Trump into another European capital submissive to Washington and Tel Aviv.

stories.title: Shenzhen Left the Gulf Out of Its Peace Declaration
stories.summary: The Gulf should take the hint. The post Shenzhen Left the Gulf Out of Its Peace Declaration appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

The three men who sat together for an hour and twenty minutes at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen lead the world’s largest nuclear powers, and between them they have a say over most of the oil that leaves the Gulf. Their four-point Declaration toward Peace did not mention Iran once. In the 48 hours before they met, American jets struck a missile launch site on Qeshm Island, Kuwait activated its air defenses against drones for the first time since early September, Bahrain fended off an Iranian attack, and a tanker burned in Hormuz off the coast of Oman. None of these developments appeared in the text.

The declaration found room for nuclear risk, United Nations reform, the immunity of state officials, and a pledge on boosting petroleum products . Ukraine was left out too, so the silence on Iran was no snub aimed at the Gulf. It was a measure of what three capitals could sign together. On Iran, they could sign very little. Trump said all three agreed that Tehran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon. Xi Jinping called for efforts to “safeguard global energy supply chain stability.” The war that has choked a sea lane carrying a fifth of global energy exports got a nod in the corridors and nothing on paper.

For the people who live along this coast, the cost of that drift is not abstract. The Gulf’s cities run on workers from Manila, Dhaka, Kerala, and Cairo, whose families at home feel every spike in fuel prices and every week of doubt about jobs and flights. Drones over Kuwait and Bahrain are their news, too.

The easy reaction in Gulf capitals is disappointment, the old feeling of great powers meeting about the region in a room where no Gulf leader sits. There is a better way to read Shenzhen. A summit that cannot agree on Iran is also a summit that cannot impose a settlement on the Gulf. A bargain over Hormuz struck by three outsiders, each with its own war and its own election calendar, would have been the worst outcome for Riyadh, Muscat, or Abu Dhabi. That bargain did not happen. In plain words, the great powers have no shared plan for this war, and the pen has passed back to the region.

Someone has already been carrying it around. Weeks before Shenzhen, Beijing quietly built the outline of a regional track. In early November, Xi hosted Sultan Haitham bin Tariq of Oman, the first visit by an Omani head of state since the two countries established ties in 1978, and their joint statement called for safe navigation to resume through Hormuz and for Washington and Tehran to restart dialogue. China’s special envoy Zhai Jun then went to Tehran and on to Muscat, where Oman’s foreign ministry said he set out China’s position on the Gulf and its implications for global security, on an itinerary that also lists Riyadh. That is not the posture of a power waiting for Washington’s permission. It is the posture of a broker working the one road that runs between Iran and its Arab neighbors.

The honest objection should be stated plainly. Beijing is no neutral referee in Tehran’s eyes or in Washington’s. China is Iran’s largest trading partner and the biggest customer of its crude, and its diplomacy has stalled more than once this year. In May, Trump came home from Beijing saying Xi wanted the strait kept open . It did not reopen.

All of that is true, and it changes less than it seems. Look at the alternatives. Washington is a combatant, and its jets were over Qeshm this week under the label of self-defense. Moscow has deepened its partnership with Iran throughout the war. Oman and Qatar have carried messages faithfully, but a messenger cannot underwrite a settlement. Of the outside powers, only Beijing buys from Tehran, trades heavily with every Gulf capital, and gains nothing from a closed strait. For obvious reasons, that combination is rare, and the Gulf would be unwise to leave it idle.

The Gulf’s own leaders have already drawn the conclusion that matters. “Geography prevails,” the UAE’s Reem Al Hashimy said in May. “We’re going to have to live with each other, the Gulf states and Iran.” Shenzhen confirmed that no one else is going to arrange that cohabitation for them.

The practical step is narrow. Gulf capitals should ask Beijing to turn Zhai’s shuttle into a standing Hormuz contact group: Oman and Saudi Arabia, plus any other Gulf state that wants a seat, along with Iran at the same table and China as convener. Its first task should be modest, a deconfliction line for commercial shipping, so that the fate of a burning tanker no longer depends on which side calls its strike self-defense. Grand bargains on enrichment and sanctions can wait for Washington and Tehran. A shipping channel cannot.

The timing favors such an ask. The U.S.-China trade truce expires on January 10 , Trump needs both a trade deal with Beijing and lower fuel prices at home, and Beijing needs the strait open for its own tankers. A Gulf proposal placed on that table before January carries weight in both capitals. Washington will probably grumble about a forum with China in the chair. It would be grumbling about a vacuum it chose not to fill in Shenzhen.

When Zhai Jun next lands in Riyadh, watch what he leaves with. If it is a statement on shipping signed by the people who live along the strait, the Gulf will have written the clause that Shenzhen left out. If it is only a round of thanks, the next tanker fire will again be settled by whoever fires last.

stories.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Tethered to Fossil Fuels
stories.summary: The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A pile of sulfur at an oil refinery in Cartagena, Spain. Sulfur, a byproduct of refining, is needed to make phosphate fertilizer. Angel Garcia / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ANALYSIS

The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout.

By Fred Pearce • November 24, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India to southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño , the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

A farmer spreads fertilizer on his land in Indian Kashmir. Firdous Nazir / NurPhoto via AP

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.

Cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Amirhosein Khorgooi / AP Photo

Most discussion about the resource implications of the Iran war has concentrated on disruption to the Gulf’s oil and natural gas exports. But the war has also hindered the production of the two most critical fertilizers in the world: nitrogen-based ammonia, which is made in the Gulf using hydrogen extracted from natural gas, and phosphate fertilizer, whose manufacture requires sulfur extracted from hydrocarbon refining. The conflict has cut the amount of nitrogen supplied to farmers by about a quarter but phosphate supplies by 40 percent.

As the war has progressed, the supply of sulfur has continued to shrink. In May, China, the world’s largest exporter of sulfuric acid, banned sales to foreign manufacturers to protect its own fertilizer supplies. Then in August, Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom’s Astrakhan gas processing plant, knocking out 60 percent of Russia’s sulfur production.

With supplies cut and prices up by more than a third, sometimes exceeding $1,000 per metric ton, much of the sulfur that has been available has been snapped up by the mining industry, which can afford the higher prices. The price hike has left phosphate fertilizer producers in a bind. Many have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, cannot pay for the product. Mosaic, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers, more than halved its U.S. production in 2026 and has announced plans to shut one plant for six months starting in December. “Without affordable sulfur,” production superintendent Hector Mier said last month, the company was “forced to curtail production. That means less fertilizer for farmers and less food grown in American farmland.” Saudi and Brazilian plants have also closed.

As less fertilizer is added to soils, says an analyst, there will be an “erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries.”

Brendan Rice, an agribusiness analyst for the Washington, D.C.-based International Food Policy Research Institute, warns that as less phosphate fertilizer is added to soils, there will be “a slow-rolling erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries” stretching through 2027 and beyond.

The first clear signs of the downturn may emerge in the next three months with the harvest of rice in India and Thailand, soy in Brazil, and corn in southern Africa. Amoah says it will “lock in grocery inflation for years.”

What will happen if the Gulf conflict continues to restrict sulfur supplies?

There is no immediate prospect of a revival of sulfur mining. Only two mines remain open: the Osiek Mine in southern Poland and the Kawah Ijen volcano on the Indonesian island of Java, where a few hundred intrepid miners armed with hand tools clamber down into the crater to dig out yellow blocks of elemental sulfur, which they haul to the surface in bamboo baskets. Neither mine could quickly increase production, analysts say. And a widespread reopening of closed mines would be a costly and risky enterprise when Gulf production of cheap sulfur could resume at least as quickly.

A miner gathers sulfur from Kawah Ijen, an active volcano on the Indonesian island of Java. Oscar Espinosa / SOPA Images / LightRocket via Getty Images

There is sulfur stockpiled at a few refineries — notably some 10 million metric tons around tar-sands deposits in the Canadian province of Alberta, some of which is sent to fertilizer manufacturers in Canada and the U.S. But scaling up distribution quickly for the international market would be challenging. “Every tonne must be excavated off the block, trucked to a melting site, melted, formed, and railed to Vancouver for vessel loading,” says Fiona Boyd , a director of London-based Acuity Commodities. “[It’s] a lengthy and expensive process.”

Experts predict that Gulf supplies of sulfur will eventually resume. But that will only postpone the day, says Maslin, when the world faces a long-term sulfur crunch as demand rises while supplies falter.

On the demand side, most observers expect a rapid increase in the use of sulfuric acid as more metals are refined to make batteries. And as the world’s population continues to rise, feeding more people will also likely require more sulfur to make more phosphorus fertilizer. Overall, Maslin sees the market growing by around 60 percent to 400 million metric tons by midcentury.

Farmers could reduce their use of synthetic fertilizers by nourishing their soils with animal manure and farm waste.

But at the same time, he says, supply is set to crash as the world’s energy system decarbonizes, with consumption peaking and then falling sharply over the next three decades, slashing the production of sulfur waste at refineries. In 2022, Maslin and his University College London colleagues calculated that shifting away from fossil fuels “could create a shortfall of sulfuric acid as large as 320 million [metric tons], or 130 percent of present-day production.”

The supply crunch would drive up the cost of sulfur, Maslin said. Then, as now, farmers — and the world’s food supply — would be the likely losers.

To address the shortfall, farmers could reduce their dependence on both nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers by nourishing their soils organically. Animal manure and organic farm wastes are rich in both chemicals. But few agriculturalists expect such methods to do more than moderate rising demand for synthetic fertilizer — and the sulfur needed to make it.

So where will the sulfur come from? We could go back to large-scale mining. Unlike some strategic materials, the world is not short of geological sulfur. It is the 13th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, found in volcanoes, salt domes, and in sedimentary deposits created by the evaporation of seawater.

A tractor spreads fertilizer on a soybean field in Goias, Brazil. Mateus Bonomi / Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

But Maslin warns of the risks. “Direct mining of elemental sulfur is dirty, toxic, [and] destructive.” To minimize the damage, he says, “the world needs to cut demand by recycling and using alternative industrial technologies that avoid intensive use of sulfuric acid.” Widespread commercial recycling of sulfur has potential. Sulfuric acid is a major component of widely used lead-acid batteries, for instance. In the U.S. it is widely recycled along with lead.

Another approach is to cut demand for sulfur’s biggest use — making phosphate fertilizer — by recycling the phosphates found in human sewage, which is where much of the material used to grow our food ends up.

More than half the world’s population is now connected to sewage systems. Sewage sludge from treatment works may contain industrial contaminants but is generally considered safe for application to cropland and often sold or given to farmers in developed countries, notably the U.K. and the U.S. Sludge incinerators in Japan and Germany sell their leftover ash, still rich in phosphates, either to farmers or to fertilizer manufacturers. Willem Schipper, a Dutch consultant in industrial chemistry, calculates that current sewage systems worldwide could deliver around a million metric tons of phosphates each year. That is roughly 3 percent of what is mined each year, but it would trim the need for both sulfur and phosphate, a rock that is itself in increasingly short supply.

By removing phosphates from raw sewage at treatment works, recycling would also reduce the environmental impacts of high levels of phosphates in rivers, where the chemical spurs the growth of plants and algae that block sunlight from penetrating the water and lower oxygen levels. So, while one version of a circular economy might falter as fossil fuels are sidelined, another, smaller circular economy could emerge.

stories.title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta
stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report
stories.summary: Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A coal mine in Jharkhand, India. Vishal Kumar Singh / AFP via Getty Images via Inside Climate News

Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations.

The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice, and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries — Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption — are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 1.5 degree C warming target in the Paris Agreement.

Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment .

The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”

Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.

“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 1.5 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”

“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”

The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.

In particular, the climate, environment, and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.

Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”

Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.

“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

— Bob Berwyn , Inside Climate News
