stories.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
stories.summary: A government-commissioned report calls for a "rebalancing" of the amount paid to different claimants.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit Published 13 hours ago

Giving a statement in the House of Commons, Sir Stephen said Pip "remains a vital source of support" but the system was "no longer fit for purpose".

He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence".

The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment.

It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve.

Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead.

In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do".

It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts.

'Rebalancing'

Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available.

But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs.

The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all.

"Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says.

"Conversely, this benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled."

The review also calls for an increase in face-to-face assessments, which has been show to reduce eligibility.

The remit of the review was not to produce savings, and it does not set out whether the reforms would reduce the overall welfare bill.

Spending on Pip is set to be about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn by the end of the decade.

It comes after a separate review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

The government welcomed Milburn's report , which included a recommendation to move under-25s off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

This has lead to concerns about a two-tier system, where some people with the same conditions could get different levels of payments depending on their age.

The government has said it will consider the Timms review alongside Milburn's recommendations, with its final proposals set out early next year.

Sir Stephen said this would include detailing the overall costs of changes to the system.

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 17 November

'Months of uncertainty'

Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said the review's recommendations had "the potential to better tailor Pip to claimants' needs".

But he said this would also create challenges, "most importantly in defining what disability-related costs are included, and finding a fair way of measuring them".

Latimer said making it easier to apply for Pip in its current form would "likely increase the number of claimants - and hence spending".

He added: "If the government wants to make Pip easier to apply for while also keeping spending in line with current projections, they would likely have to tighten eligibility criteria or reduce award amounts."

Disability charities have largely welcomed the review's recommendations of fast-tracked support and fewer reassessments.

However, they have said any changes should not leave disabled people financially worse off.

The Liberal Democrats said younger disabled people would now face "months of uncertainty" whilst the government considers the separate reviews from Timms and Milburn, and urged ministers to say quickly what they intend to do.

Reform UK's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Timms' recommendations will not cut the ballooning benefits bill so taxes on working people will inevitably rise."

He said his party would "bring back rigorous in-person assessments and ensure benefits are only available for British people" in order to lower the welfare bill.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales. However, the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

Huw Irranca-Davies gave a passionate speech to the Senedd in defence of his role

Published 24 November 2026

An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's Presiding Officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies.

Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29.

Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.

Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially".

Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down."

A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.

Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties.

"The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said.

"Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities.

"Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard. "Without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting."

After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced".

"We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon

At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon . Martin was not among them.

Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?"

"It's been a little bit duller without us in here," she added.

In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".

Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November.

The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.

The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.

Reform's Welsh leader Helen Jenner attempted to force the Senedd's presiding officer to quit

Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.

She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".

"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.

"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.

"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.

"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."

The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.

A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.

Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".

"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.

"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.

"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

stories.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
stories.summary: Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

Andy Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators Published 23 July

More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024 Published 16 September

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.

She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".

She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.

"Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."

In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10.

"I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said.

"It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."

Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".

Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content.

"It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."

They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".

Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.

A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.

One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.

A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

stories.body:
The UK government has issued a warning and advice for any companies that support Ukraine's armed forces

Published 24 November 2026

The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert , external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".

When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".

Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.

The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

stories.body:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.

The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.

The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.

The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

stories.title: Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit
stories.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has published his review of the personal independence payment (Pip), along with recommended changes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence".

The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales.

The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled.

Here's what you need to know.

Pip benefit system 'not fit for purpose' and 'dehumanising' assessments should change, review finds - follow live

The current Pip process does not work

This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign.

While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review.

The review recommends both short and long term changes

First the short term.

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Then the long term.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.

The review does not propose benefits cuts

The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.

The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.

Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

How does this report sit with the Milburn review that was published last week?

Alan Milburn's report - which proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK - recommended that Pip be removed from people under 25 as part of a package of measures to tackle youth unemployment.

Today's review does not make the same recommendation. It will be up to the government to decide how they marry the two reports. They have said they are committed to reforming the Pip assessment process, but what that means in practice probably won't be known until the New Year when they publish their considered response.

stories.title: Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn
stories.summary: The party says the move could fund the construction of modern purpose-built prisons elsewhere.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Wandsworth prison, in south London, is among those that would be closed by the Conservatives

Published 24 November 2026

London's Victorian jails should be closed down and the land sold off to property developers, the Conservatives have said, as they launched a plan to massively increase prison places in England and Wales.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said the move could raise £1.4bn to help fund the construction of "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere".

He claimed a Tory government would create 50,000 extra prison places within "six or seven years" and end Labour's early release scheme in its first term in office.

Labour said nobody would believe the Tory plan "given they only added a dismal 500 places while in government".

Speaking at a press conference in Westminster, Timothy said it was "fair" to highlight the previous Conservartive government's failure to significantly increase prison places.

But he insisted "this is a different generation of Conservative politicians under Kemi [Badenoch]'s leadership, and we are making different choices".

Unlike previous Tory-led administrations, they were being "explicit" about which departmental budgets they would cut - international aid, culture and the Cabinet Office - to fund new prisons, he added.

Under the Tory plans, an extra £2bn a year would go to the Ministry of Justice to pay for what Timothy called "the largest prison-building programme in modern history".

"It will let us end Labour's early release schemes once and for all, and bring back shorter sentences to lock up criminals like shoplifters," he added.

He told the audience "prison works" because it kept criminals off the street and he was "deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation".

The Conservatives are setting up a commission, chaired by former minister Sir Simon Clarke, to work out how to speed up the building of new prisons by removing obstacles in the planning, procurement and judicial systems.

The review would also look at "how to get out of the old Victorian prison estate, starting in London," Timothy said in his speech.

Prisons such as Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville "sit on some of the most valuable land in the world," he added.

"Getting out of these sites is not only a good idea in itself. It will free up land for residential use in London, where our housing shortage is most acute."

He said the Tories would "strip back regulations, like affordable housing quotas and listed status, to give the land its highest realisable value," but it would only sell off the land when "market conditions are favourable to the taxpayer".

This could raise more than £1.4bn which would go towards building new prisons "in addition to" the 50,000 places the party has already pledged to build , he added.

The previous Conservative government set out plans to sell off London's Victorian jails, but this was ditched by Boris Johnson's administration in 2019 because of the shortage of prison places.

A Labour spokesperson said: "When it comes to leaving the prisons estate on the verge of collapse, the Tories are guilty as charged.

"They should be apologising to victims of crime who they badly let down rather than spending time lecturing others who are fixing the mess they left behind."

The Labour government was "delivering the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era so victims of crime get the justice they deserve," they added.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Published 23 November 2026

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.

But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.

Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.

However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.

But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.

Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.

Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 1 day ago

The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.

The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

"Probably so," Trump said.

Trump's personal Nvidia investments

Since returning last year to the White House, the president has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia.

Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang Published 1 day ago

Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, Prof Stuart Russell, told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Concerns remain among US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible".

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to give evidence before the Senate banking committee.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said the reinstatement was "reckless".

And the chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Delegation of 50 to accompany minister, with trip criticised after universities were warned about Chinese interference

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is travelling to Beijing this week to promote UK education, weeks after MI5 issued a rare public warning to universities about Chinese interference in UK academia.

A 50-strong UK delegation, including 18 university leaders, will accompany the minister when she attends the first UK-China education summit in nine years, aimed at opening up new opportunities for universities, colleges and education businesses.

The visit prompted criticism, as it comes two months after UK universities were warned by MI5 that China’s intelligence services were using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal secrets from hi-tech projects.

One critic described Powell’s visit, which begins on Tuesday, as “mind-blowingly shortsighted”, while the Conservatives said the education secretary’s priorities were “all wrong”.

Discussions in China are expected to cover higher education, technical and vocational education, schools, English language teaching, digital education and education technology, the Department for Education (DfE) said

“The freedom and independence of our academic institutions is sacrosanct,” a DfE spokesperson said. “We will not accept collaborations which compromise our national security or attempt to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with UK universities.”

Successive British governments have welcomed Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation between the two countries. About 150,000 Chinese students currently study at UK universities, contributing £7bn to the UK economy every year. Concerns have been growing in recent years, however, about the potential risks of such close collaboration.

On 30 September, MI5 warned vice-chancellors that a Chinese state-owned conglomerate called the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) had funded 100 or more academics in return for access to research which found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

The claim was denied by the Chinese embassy. Before that there was outcry when it emerged Sheffield Hallam University had complied with a demand from Beijing to halt research about human rights abuses in China .

Condemning the trip to China, the shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said Powell’s priorities were all wrong. “Instead of seeking closer ties to China, Powell should clamp down on CCP [Chinese Communist party] attempts to influence our own universities & its treatment of those who criticise it,” she posted on X.

Luke de Pulford, the executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, wrote on X: “Mind-blowingly shortsighted in policy terms.”

“What might seem to the uninitiated like an economic opportunity, or short-term hope to plug a gap in finances may actually be the government signing UK high education’s death warrant.

“If the balance tips too far towards dependence; if Beijing gets enough leverage, these institutions will cease to operate freely, and continue to leak IP and sensitive research to an adversary.”

after newsletter promotion

Sam Dunning, the director of UK-China Transparency, said the UK was in unprecedented territory. “British universities have never been so financially dependent on foreign students as they are today on Chinese students,” he said.

“Nor have there ever been more foreign nationals from any one country than British nationals studying Stem at an elite level in our top institutions, as is the case with China today.

“We are in unprecedented territory and on perilous terrain. The public interest demands careful, long-term thinking about these issues, and not continued short-termism.”

The summit forms part of government plans to grow education exports to £40bn a year by 2030. “British education is one of our country’s greatest strengths,” said Powell. “Expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.

“Education builds lasting relationships and creates opportunities, but it also gives us the relationships and channels we need to have open and honest conversations. That is why we are putting education at the heart of clear-eyed engagement with China, using Britain’s world-class reputation to support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

stories.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
stories.summary: Claire Waxman tells the BBC Andy Burnham needs to put justice in his 10-year plan for government.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Claire Waxman said the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe

Published 24 November 2026

The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

'Very poor' letters

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme , the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system.

'Broken system'

As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system.

The survey report will argue this would improve coordination between different agencies, as well as allowing victims to monitor when they will access the various legal rights they have under the Victims' Code.

It will also call for an "end-to-end" review of how victims navigate the system, similar to recent reviews that have focused on sentencing or the courts.

Responding to the survey results, Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government was doing "everything we can to fix the broken system we inherited".

She added that ministers had already taken steps to improve the court backlog, and would be publishing an update to the Victims' Code next year.

She said this would be easier for victims to understand, and would set "clear expectations for criminal justice agencies and help victims feel supported".
